inline.s: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should, until they become Buddhas, be deficient or incomplete in any of their faculties, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(41. All Faculties Complete)
If I become a Buddha,
and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should, until they become Buddhas, be deficient or incomplete in any of their faculties, then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should all fail to obtain the samādhi of purity and liberation; and if, dwelling in that samādhi, in the space of a single thought they should fail to make offerings to immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, without losing their concentration — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(42. Dwelling in Samādhi, Making Offerings to Buddhas)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should fail to obtain the samādhi of purity and liberation — dwelling in that samādhi, in the space of a single thought making offerings to immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, without losing their concentration — then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should, after the end of their lives, fail to be born into noble families — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(43. Hearing the Name, Attaining Blessings)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should after the end of their lives fail to be born into noble families — if this should not be so, then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should not leap with joy, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and perfect the roots of virtue — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(44. Perfecting the Roots of Virtue)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should not leap with joy, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and perfect the roots of virtue (roots of goodness) — if this should not be so, then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should all fail to obtain the samādhi of universal equality; and if, dwelling in that samādhi, until they become Buddhas, they should fail constantly to behold immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(45. The Samādhi of Universal Equality)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should all fail to obtain the samādhi of universal equality — dwelling in that samādhi, until they become Buddhas, constantly beholding immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas — then I shall not become a Buddha.
[The samādhi of universal equality] One who cultivates this concentration can, within that samādhi, behold all Buddhas everywhere.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows, should fail to hear at will the Dharma they wish to hear — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(46. Hearing the Dharma According to One's Vow)
If I become a Buddha,
and the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows, should fail to hear at will the Dharma they wish to hear — if this should not be so, then I shall not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should fail immediately to attain non-retrogression — may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(47. Hearing the Name, Attaining Non-Retrogression)
If I become a Buddha,
and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should fail immediately to attain the stage of non-retrogression, then I shall not become a Buddha.
[The stage of non-retrogression] Also rendered as avaivartika, or as Apidha (
pí

)bazhi — that is, Aparivartya. This is the name of a bodhisattva stage. A bodhisattva must cultivate for one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa before he can reach this stage. From that point on there is only advance, step by step, until Buddhahood; in between there is no falling back. The Sutra of Amitābha Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, says:
“The sentient beings who are born in the Land of Utmost Bliss are all avaivartika.”

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should fail immediately to reach the first, the second, and the third Dharma-patience, and should be unable immediately to attain non-retrogression with respect to all Buddha-Dharmas — may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(48. Attaining the Three Dharma-Patiences)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should fail immediately to reach the first, the second, and the third Dharma-patience, and should be unable immediately to attain non-retrogression with respect to all Buddha-Dharmas, then I shall not become a Buddha.

[The first, the second, and the third Dharma-patience] Namely, the patience of sound and echo, the patience of gentle compliance, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. For a detailed commentary on these three kinds of patience, see “15. The Bodhi Site.”
[The Buddha told Ānanda: Then the bhikṣu Dharmākara, having spoken these vows, spoke in gāthās:
I establish a resolve surpassing the world,
(I must fully realize the fruit of Buddhahood)
and if these vows are not fulfilled
(if these forty-eight vows are not fulfilled)
, I swear I shall not attain perfect Enlightenment
(I swear I shall not become a Buddha)

[A resolve surpassing the world] This is the resolve spoken of earlier: “surpassing the lands of countless Buddhas.” [Perfect Enlightenment] True awakening; becoming a Buddha is called attaining perfect Enlightenment. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ānanda: When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this gāthā, he addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘Just so, World-Honored One! I have brought forth the mind of unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the Dharma of the scriptures for me; I shall cultivate accordingly and gather in a pure and adorned, immeasurable, wondrous Buddha-land. Grant that in this world I may swiftly attain perfect Enlightenment and uproot the very source of the toil and suffering of birth and death.’”
Again, as a great donor I shall relieve all who are poor and suffering, and cause all those multitudes of beings to be free from sorrow and affliction through the long night.
Bringing forth all roots of goodness and accomplishing the fruit of bodhi — when I attain perfect Enlightenment, my name shall be Immeasurable Life.
[Immeasurable Life] This is a Buddha's name; its transliteration is Amita.
When beings hear this name
(when beings hear this name and title)
, they all come to my land; their bodies are of the Buddha's golden hue, and all their marvelous marks are complete.
And with a heart of great compassion they benefit all the multitudes of beings,
(causing them)
to leave desire behind, to dwell in profound right mindfulness, and to cultivate the pure conduct of the holy life with pure wisdom.
[Multitudes of beings] Sentient beings.
May the light of my wisdom universally illumine the lands of the ten directions, dispelling the darkness of the three defilements and rescuing beings from all their woes.

[The three defilements] Another name for the three poisons, namely greed, hatred, and delusion. [The darkness of the three defilements] The darkness of the three poisons. [Rescuing beings from all their woes] Rescuing sentient beings from all their woes by the light of wisdom.
Causing all to renounce the sufferings of the three evil paths, to extinguish the darkness of the afflictions, to open the eye of wisdom for them, and to gain the body of light.

[The three paths] The path of blood, the path of knives, and the path of fire. The path of blood is the animal realm, because animals dwell where they are constantly killed or devour one another; the path of knives is the realm of hungry ghosts, because hungry ghosts dwell where hunger and the coercion of swords, whips, and staves are constant; the path of fire is the hell realm, because hells are places of constant freezing cold or of scorching by fierce fire. These three paths are another name for the three evil paths.
Shutting off
(closing)
all evil paths, opening up
(throwing open)
the gate of good destinies, opening the Dharma-treasury for the multitudes, and bestowing abundantly the treasure of merit and virtue.

[Evil paths] As the world's people understand it, the evil paths are the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; but the evil paths spoken of here are the five evil paths named in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) — hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. “Shutting off all evil paths” means cutting off the road of birth-and-death transmigration. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“Each should diligently and vigorously strive, and seek it for himself with all his might. He will surely transcend and pass beyond, and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, the roads of those destinies are naturally closed.”

[The five evil paths] Namely: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Because these five paths are the road of birth-and-death transmigration, for a cultivator who would end birth and death and escape the three realms they are all evil paths.
[Good destinies] “Good destinies” here does not mean the three good paths among the six paths (gods, humans, and asuras), but rather the ending of the road of birth-and-death transmigration.
[Opening the Dharma-treasury for the multitudes] Teaching sentient beings to reveal their own intrinsic nature (the Dharma-treasury).

[Dharma-treasury] Also called the treasury of Buddha-Dharmas, or the Tathāgata-garbha; that is, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, which contains and holds all the merits of the Tathāgata's fruition-ground. (See in full
“Heart, Intrinsic Nature, Tathāgata-garbha”
Like the Buddha's unobstructed wisdom, practicing deeds of kindness and compassion, always acting as teacher of gods and humans, and becoming the hero of the three realms.
Proclaiming the Dharma with a lion's roar, broadly delivering all sentient beings, fulfilling the vows made in the past
(perfectly accomplishing the forty-eight great vows made in former days)
, and causing all to become Buddhas
(causing all beings born in my land to become Buddhas)

[The lion's roar] The Buddha proclaims the Dharma without the least fear, his voice shaking the ten directions, so that all demons are awed into submission — as when the lion roars and a hundred beasts submit.
[All becoming Buddhas] Causing all sentient beings born in my land to become Buddhas. This is as the forty-eight vows above say:

“All sentient beings, and those in the realm of Yama, and those in the three evil paths, who come to be born in my land and receive the transforming influence of my Dharma, shall all accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If these vows attain their fruit
(if these vows are to be accomplished)
, the great chiliocosm should tremble in response
(the great chiliocosm should tremble in response)
, and all the gods of the heavens should rain down rare and wondrous flowers.]

[The Buddha told Ānanda: When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this gāthā, the whole earth immediately trembled in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself in the air, with voices of praise saying: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this gāthā, the whole earth immediately trembled in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers as if falling rain, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself in the air, with voices of praise saying: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment (he is certain to become a Buddha).

[The six kinds of trembling] The six signs of auspicious trembling, namely: moving, surging, quaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. These six kinds of trembling can be known and seen only by one who has the divine eye; ordinary beings know nothing of them. [The voices of praise in the air: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment] Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara declared in his forty-eight vows: if any one of these vows is not fulfilled, I swear I shall not become a Buddha. “The voices of praise in the air: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment” is a prophecy: the bhikṣu Dharmākara will certainly become a Buddha, and all forty-eight vows will be fulfilled.
This chapter teaches: the bhikṣu Dharmākara, through cultivation over immeasurable kalpas, accumulated merit and virtue, and thereby brought forth the Buddha-land (
“sensing and attaining a vast and pure dwelling-place”
) — the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.

[Ānanda, when the bhikṣu Dharmākara had brought forth these vast and mighty vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, and in the midst of all the multitudes of gods and humans, he dwelt in true wisdom, courageous and vigorous, single-mindedly and devotedly adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was open and vast, supreme and uniquely wondrous, established and ever constant, without decay or change.]

Ānanda, after the bhikṣu Dharmākara had brought forth these forty-eight great vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and in the midst of all the multitudes of gods and humans, he dwelt in true wisdom and cultivated with courage and vigor, always single-mindedly and devotedly adorning the Buddha-land (the wondrous land) with the immeasurable, boundless merits of the fruition of awakening. The Buddha-land he was to cultivate was open and broad, magnificent and vast, supreme and uniquely wondrous, altogether foremost. It is ever constant and unchanging, never decaying or growing old.

[The Buddha-land he cultivated] The Buddha-land he cultivated was brought forth and made manifest by the immeasurable, boundless merits of the fruition of awakening of the bhikṣu Dharmākara. The Vajraśekhara Sutra says:
“This Buddha-land alone is made entirely pure by the vajra-nature itself.”
[Established and ever constant, without decay or change] The Buddha-land he cultivated (the Land of Utmost Bliss), once established, is forever thus; it has no marks of decay or damage.

[Through immeasurable kalpas, he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, hatred, delusion, or desire, and was unattached to sights, sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects. He delighted only in recollecting the roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he planted the roots of all virtues, counting no hardships.]

Through immeasurable kalpas the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, hatred, delusion, or desire, nor was he attached to the objects of the six dusts. He delighted only in recollecting the goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he cultivated the roots of all virtues, counting no hardship or difficulty as too great.
Through immeasurable kalpas, he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct
] The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:
“Through inconceivable koṭis of kalpas, he accumulated and planted the immeasurable virtuous conduct of a bodhisattva.”

A bodhisattva needs only three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas to become a Buddha, yet the bhikṣu Dharmākara passed through immeasurable kalpas before completing the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. From this we can see how great the difficulty was — and therefore how incomparably supreme the Western Land of Utmost Bliss is! [The six dusts] The dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of scent, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, and the dust of mental objects. “Dust” means defilement; it is so called because it can defile the human mind and prevent the true nature from manifesting. It is also called the six objects, the outer objects perceived by the six sense-faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). [Ultimate truth] The true principle of the stillness of nirvāṇa as seen by sagely wisdom is called ultimate truth.

[Having few desires and knowing contentment, he sought only the pure Dharma and benefited the multitudes of beings. His resolve never flagged, and his power of patience was perfected. Toward all sentient beings he always bore kindness and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words he exhorted, instructed, and urged them on. He reverenced the Three Jewels, served his teachers, and had no heart of falseness or flattery.]

He had few desires and knew contentment, seeking only the good Dharma and benefiting the multitudes of beings. His resolve never flagged, and his power of patience was perfected. Toward all sentient beings he always bore kindness and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words he exhorted, instructed, and urged them on. He reverenced the Three Jewels and served his teachers, without any heart of falseness or flattery.
[Pure Dharma] The general name for all good dharmas. [The power of patience] The power of patient endurance. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Again I see the Buddha's disciples dwelling in the power of patience; when arrogant people revile and beat them, they are able to endure it all, seeking the Buddha-Way.”
[Kindness and patience] Compassion and patient endurance. [Exhort and instruct] To admonish and to make clear. [Urge them on] To encourage and cause them to advance.

[Adorning all practices, his norms and models were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory transformations, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded his mouth-karma well and did not ridicule the faults of others; he guarded his body-karma well and did not transgress the precepts and rules; he guarded his mind-karma well and was pure and undefiled. To all lands, cities, settlements, kin, and treasures he was wholly unattached. Constantly, by giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — the practices of the six pāramitās — he taught, established, and settled sentient beings in the unsurpassed, true Way.]

The bhikṣu Dharmākara adorned all practices, and his norms and models were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory transformations, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded his mouth-karma well and did not ridicule the faults of others; he guarded his body-karma well and did not transgress the precepts and rules; he guarded his mind-karma well and was pure and undefiled. To all lands, cities, settlements, kin, and treasures he was wholly unattached. Always, by giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — the wondrous practices of the six pāramitās — he taught, established, and settled sentient beings, causing them to dwell in the unsurpassed, true Way.

[Norms and models] The standard that conduct ought to follow. [Contemplating all dharmas as illusory transformations] Contemplating all dharmas as being like magical illusions. [Precepts and rules] The precepts are the moral code; the rules are the ceremonial norms — what a cultivator must follow in establishing himself and dealing with the world.

[Because he accomplished such roots of goodness, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response. Sometimes he was an elder or a householder, of a wealthy clan and honored estate; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage emperor; sometimes a lord of the six heavens of desire, and even a Brahmā king. In the presence of all Buddhas he honored and made offerings without ever ceasing. Such merit as this cannot be fully told.]

Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara accomplished such roots of goodness, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures welled up naturally. In his successive lives he was sometimes an elder or a householder, of a wealthy clan and honored estate; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage king; sometimes a lord of the various heavens of the realm of desire, and even the great Brahmā king of the realm of form. In the presence of all Buddhas he honored and made offerings without ever ceasing. Such merit as this cannot be fully told.

[Immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response] Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated over many kalpas the merit of giving and of keeping the precepts, treasures appeared in response, welling up naturally. [Elder] A general term for one who has accumulated wealth and possesses virtue. [Kṣatriya] That is, kṣatriya, the second of the four Indian castes. [The four castes] Brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra. The brāhmaṇas were the priests of ancient India and held the highest authority; the kṣatriyas were the royal class, honored as were the brāhmaṇas; the vaiśyas were the ordinary class of workers, farmers, and merchants; the śūdras were slaves who served others. [The six heavens of desire] The realm of desire (the world in which beings dwell who have the two desires of lust and food) has six heavens, hence the name: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, and the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others' Transformations. [Lord of the six heavens of desire] The lord of each heaven of the realm of desire. [Brahmā king] An abbreviation of Great Brahmā King. [The realm of form] Above the realm of desire. Because the beings of this realm have only a physical body and are free of the two desires of lust and food, it is called the realm of form.

[Sometimes a lord of the various heavens of the realm of desire, and even the great Brahmā king of the realm of form] The Sutra of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment (the Song translation) says:
“Ānanda, the monk Dharmākara
(the bhikṣu Dharmākara)

, when he practiced the bodhisattva practices, honored and reverenced and made offerings in the presence of all Buddhas without ever ceasing. As a great king of the Four Heavens, he constantly went to the Buddha's presence, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a king of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, he constantly went to the Buddha's presence, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a king of the Yāma Heaven, a king of the Tuṣita Heaven, a king of the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, a king of the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others' Transformations, and even as a great Brahmā king, he constantly went to the Buddha's presence, reverently bowing and making offerings.”
[From body and mouth there constantly came immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like sandalwood
(zhān)

and the utpala flower; its fragrance universally perfumed immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his countenance was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty subsidiary characteristics were all complete. From his hands there constantly came inexhaustible treasures, adornments, and all necessities — the very finest things — bringing benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition he was able to cause immeasurable sentient beings all to bring forth the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

By the response of his merit, from the body and mouth of the bhikṣu Dharmākara there constantly came of themselves immeasurable wondrous fragrances, like sandalwood and the utpala flower, whose fragrance universally perfumed immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his countenance was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty subsidiary characteristics were all complete. From his hands there constantly came inexhaustible treasures, adornments, and all necessities — the very finest things — to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition he was able to cause immeasurable sentient beings all to bring forth the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[The eighty subsidiary characteristics] Also called the eighty minor marks, namely: an invisible uṣṇīṣa; a high nose without visible nostrils; eyebrows like the new moon; ear-lobes hanging down; a body firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa's; joints like hook and chain; the body turning at once like an elephant king's; when walking, the feet raised four inches from the ground, leaving an imprint; nails the color of red copper, thin and lustrous; knee-bones firm, round, and fine; a clean body; a soft body; an unbending body; fingers round and slender; the lines of the fingers hidden; veins deep and invisible; ankles invisible; a lustrous body; the body self-possessed and not bent; a full and complete body; a complete and sufficient countenance; an abiding-place so stable that none can disturb it; majesty shaking all; all beings rejoicing to see him; a face neither long nor large; a countenance upright and unfaltering in color; face and eyes complete; lips the color of the bimba fruit; a voice deep and far-reaching; a navel deep, round, and fine; hair curling to the right; hands and feet complete; hands and feet compliant; hand-lines bright and straight; hand-lines long; hand-lines unbroken; all beings of evil mind becoming gentle and joyful upon seeing him; a broad and exceedingly fair face; a face pure and full as the moon; speaking gently and joyfully according to the minds of beings; fragrance issuing from the pores; supreme fragrance issuing from the mouth; a bearing like the lion's; advancing and resting like the elephant king's; a gait like the goose king's; a head like the mādana fruit; every part of the voice complete; four teeth white and sharp; a red tongue; a thin tongue; red hair; hair soft and clean; eyes broad and long; all the marks of the gate of death complete; hands and feet red and white like the color of the lotus; a navel that does not protrude; a belly not visible; a slender belly; a body that does not sway; a body of weight; a large body; a tall body; hands and feet soft, clean, and smooth; the light at his four sides a fathom long; walking with light shining from his body; looking upon beings with equality; not despising beings; not increasing or diminishing with the voices of beings; teaching the Dharma without attachment; teaching the Dharma according to the languages of beings; uttering sounds that respond to beings; teaching the Dharma in sequence by cause and condition; all beings unable to exhaust the contemplation of his marks; contemplation that never wearies; hair long and fine; hair not disordered; hair curling beautifully; hair the color of blue pearls; hands and feet bearing the marks of virtue.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: The bhikṣu Dharmākara cultivated the bodhisattva practices and accumulated merit and virtue beyond measure or bound. He attained mastery over all dharmas, which is not something that can be known by speech and discrimination. The vows he made were perfectly accomplished, and he abides in accordance with reality in a pure Buddha-land complete in adornment and vast in awesome virtue.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: The bhikṣu Dharmākara cultivated the bodhisattva practices and accumulated merit and virtue beyond measure or bound. He attained mastery over all dharmas; this is not something that can be known by speech and discrimination. The forty-eight great vows he made were perfectly accomplished, and he abides in accordance with reality in a pure Buddha-land complete in adornment and vast in awesome virtue.

[When Ānanda heard what the Buddha said, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: The Bodhisattva Dharmākara who attained bodhi — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or is he a Buddha now present in some other world?]

When Ānanda heard what the Buddha said, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: The Bodhisattva Dharmākara who became a Buddha — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a present Buddha dwelling in some other world?

[The World-Honored One told him: That Tathāgata comes from nowhere, and goes nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished; he is not past, present, or future. But to repay his vows and deliver sentient beings, he is now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here, in a world named Utmost Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since he attained Buddhahood. He is now present, teaching the Dharma, surrounded in reverence by immeasurable, countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.]

The World-Honored One told Ānanda: That Tathāgata (Amitābha Buddha) comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished; he is not a Buddha of the past, not a Buddha of the present, not a Buddha of the future. But to repay his vows and broadly deliver sentient beings,
he is now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here

, in a world named Utmost Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since he attained Buddhahood. He is now present, teaching the Dharma, surrounded in reverence by immeasurable, countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

[That Tathāgata comes from nowhere, and goes nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished; he is not past, present, or future] This is the ultimate truth, spoken with respect to the true nature of all dharmas.
[He is now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here] The Assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus (the Tang translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ānanda: A hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands to the West of here, there is a world named Utmost Bliss. The bhikṣu Dharmākara attained Buddhahood there, with the name Immeasurable Life, and is now present, teaching the Dharma.”
The Sutra of Amitābha Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, says:

“The Buddha told the Elder Śāriputra: Passing from here to the West through a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is a world named Utmost Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha, named Amitābha, who is now present, teaching the Dharma.”
[Ten kalpas have passed since he attained Buddhahood] The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“Ānanda asked the Buddha: Has the Bodhisattva Dharmākara already become a Buddha and entered extinction? Has he not yet become a Buddha? Is he now present? The Buddha told Ānanda: The Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now become a Buddha. He is present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of lands from here, and his Buddha-world is named Peace and Bliss. Ānanda asked again: How long has it been since that Buddha attained the Way? The Buddha said: Since he attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed.”
The Sutra of Amitābha Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, says:
“Ten kalpas have passed since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood.”
[Amitābha] Amita; rendered in Chinese as Immeasurable. The Xuanying Yinyi says: “Amitābha is translated as Immeasurable.”
The World-Honored One's answer has two aspects, the principle and the event. As to the principle:
“That Tathāgata comes from nowhere, and goes nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished; he is not past, present, or future.”
As to the event:

“But to repay his vows and deliver sentient beings, he is now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here, in a world named Utmost Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since he attained Buddhahood. He is now present, teaching the Dharma, surrounded in reverence by immeasurable, countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.”

[The Buddha declared that Amitābha Buddha, as a bodhisattva, sought and obtained these vows. Then Prince Ajātaśatru and five hundred sons of elders, hearing it, were all filled with great joy. Each took a golden flower-canopy and together came before the Buddha to pay reverence. Having offered the flower-canopies to the Buddha, they withdrew and sat to one side to hear the sutra, and in their minds they made this vow: When we become Buddhas, may we all be like Amitābha Buddha.]

The World-Honored One proclaimed how Amitābha Buddha, when he was a bodhisattva, through accumulating merit and virtue, perfectly accomplished the forty-eight great vows. At that time Prince Ajātaśatru and five hundred sons of elders, hearing it, were all filled with great joy. Each took a golden flower-canopy, and together they came before the Buddha to pay reverence. Having made offerings of the flower-canopies to the Buddha, they sat to one side to hear the sutra, and in their minds they made this vow: When we become Buddhas, may we all be as supremely wonderful as Amitābha Buddha.
[Prince Ajātaśatru and five hundred sons of elders] The Sutra of the Pure and Immeasurable, Equal and Enlightened One Spoken by the Buddha (the Han translation) says:

“The Buddha knew it, and told the assembly of bhikṣus: This Prince Ajātaśatru and these five hundred sons of elders, after countless kalpas from now, shall all become Buddhas, like the Buddha Immeasurable Purity.”

[The Buddha knew it at once, and told the bhikṣus: This prince and the others shall later become Buddhas. In former lives they dwelt in the bodhisattva path, and through countless kalpas they have made offerings to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas. In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha they were my disciples; now they make offerings to me — we meet again. Then all the bhikṣus who heard the Buddha's words rejoiced on their behalf.]

The World-Honored One knew at once the vow in their minds and told the bhikṣus: Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders shall later become Buddhas. In former lives they dwelt in the bodhisattva path, and through countless kalpas they have made offerings to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas. In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha they were my disciples; today they come to make offerings to me, and so we meet again. Then all the bhikṣus who heard the Buddha's words rejoiced on their behalf.

[The rewards of the Land of Utmost Bliss] The dependent reward and the direct reward of the Land of Utmost Bliss. [The direct reward] The body and mind of sentient beings; this is the direct substance of the karmic fruit summoned and sensed by past karmic causes. [The dependent reward] The fruit that the body and mind depend upon and dwell in — lands, earth, houses, implements, and so on — that is, the conditions of life.
[The land adorned and pure] The land
adorned and pure.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: That realm of Utmost Bliss has immeasurable merit and is complete in adornment. Forever free of the very names of all sufferings, all calamities, evil destinies, and the afflictions of demons. Nor is there any difference of the four seasons, of cold and heat, of rain and gloom. It is peaceful, harmonious, and attuned, with joy beyond compare.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda: The Land of Utmost Bliss has immeasurable merit and is complete in adornment. Forever free of the very names of all sufferings, all calamities (the eight difficulties), evil paths (the three evil paths), and the afflictions of demons (since there is not even the name, how much less the thing itself). Nor is there any difference of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, of excessive cold and heat, of rainy days and cloudy days. It is peaceful, harmonious, and comfortable, with joy and gladness beyond compare.

[All sufferings] The various kinds of suffering. Classified, there are three sufferings, eight sufferings, ten sufferings, and a hundred and ten sufferings. [The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditionedness. First, the suffering of suffering: beings in this world already have a body of birth and death, which is suffering enough; when all sufferings press and scorch them besides, it is suffering added to suffering, and so it is called the suffering of suffering. Second, the suffering of change: the suffering felt when a state of bliss that has arisen by chance is lost. Third, the suffering of conditionedness: the suffering of all formations being impermanent, flowing on without cease, and never able to abide in stability. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth — the pain of being born; second, the suffering of old age — the pain of age and declining strength; third, the suffering of illness — the pain of sickness; fourth, the suffering of death — the pain of dying; fifth, the suffering of parting from what one loves — the pain of separation from those one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting what one hates — the pain of being together with enemies; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks — the pain of wishes unfulfilled; eighth, the suffering of the five aggregates burning — the pain that, because the illusory body and mind and all dharmas of the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness) give rise to delusion and create karma amid the objects of the six dusts, one is scorched and tormented as if by blazing fire, without cease. [The ten sufferings and the hundred and ten sufferings] As for the ten sufferings and the hundred and ten sufferings, Master Lianchi's Commentary and Notes on the Sutra of Amitābha Buddha says:

“As for the ten sufferings, the Sutra of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka says: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; and so on to the tenth, the suffering of the flow of birth and death. As for the hundred and ten sufferings, the Yogācārabhūmi says: first, the suffering of undifferentiated flow; second, the suffering of desire; third, the suffering of delusion; and so on to the fifty-fifth suffering; then nine kinds of suffering, and within those nine, further opened out in turn into fifty-five, which together make a hundred and ten sufferings.”

[The eight difficulties] Eight places and situations in which there are obstacles to seeing and hearing the Buddha-Dharma, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, Uttarakuru, the Heaven of No-Thought, being blind, deaf, or mute, worldly wisdom and clever argument, and before the Buddha or after the Buddha. Among these, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals belong to the three evil paths, and because their karmic obstacles are too heavy it is very hard for them to see and hear the Buddha-Dharma; the people of Uttarakuru have great blessings but do not understand the Buddha-Dharma, and so cannot end birth and death; the Heaven of No-Thought is a place where non-Buddhists are born, and the people there likewise cannot end birth and death; those afflicted with blindness, deafness, or muteness naturally cannot see or hear the Buddha-Dharma; worldly wisdom and clever argument means that worldly people rely on their petty cleverness, refuse to cultivate with a humble mind, and may even slander the Buddha-Dharma; and to be born before the Buddha's appearance in the world or after the Buddha's nirvāṇa is to be unable to see the Buddha or hear the Buddha-Dharma.

[The afflictions of demons] The harm wrought by demons (the four demons). [The four demons] The demon of afflictions, the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of death, and the demon of the heavens. The demon of afflictions means that habits such as greed, hatred, and delusion can torment body and mind; the demon of the five aggregates means that the five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness can produce all sufferings; the demon of death means that death can cut off the root of a person's life; the demon of the heavens means the heavenly demons and non-Buddhists who can ruin people's good works. [Mount Sumeru] Rendered in Chinese as Wondrous High Mountain, the center of a small world. This mountain is made of the four treasures of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli; no other mountain can compare with its height, and it is the king of mountains.

[In that land there are no seas, but there are many rivers. There are no hills, pits, thorns, or gravel, no mountains of iron enclosure, Sumeru, earth, or stone. Only the natural seven treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and tridacna
(chē qú)

— and carnelian are combined to make its ground, broad, level, and upright, without limit or bound. It is subtle and wondrous, rare and beautiful, pure and adorned, surpassing all the worlds of the ten directions.]

There are no seas there, but many rivers. There are no hills, pits, thorns, or gravel, no mountains made of iron enclosure, Sumeru, earth, or stone. It is made entirely of the natural seven treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, tridacna, and carnelian — combined into its ground, broad, level, and upright, boundless and without limit. The Land of Utmost Bliss is subtle and wondrous, rare and beautiful, pure and adorned, surpassing all the worlds of the ten directions.
[In that land there are no seas, but there are many rivers]
The Assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus (the Tang translation) says:

“In that realm of Utmost Bliss there are no seas, but there are many rivers. The narrowest of the rivers is fully ten yojanas wide. The shallowest of the waters is twelve yojanas deep. The depth and breadth of such rivers measure twenty, thirty, even a hundred; and some are exceedingly deep and broad, reaching a thousand yojanas.”
The Sutra of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment (the Song translation) says:

“In that Buddha-land, though there is no great ocean, there are springs and rivers flowing and mingling everywhere. Their waters are ten yojanas, twenty yojanas, thirty yojanas, even a hundred thousand yojanas broad, and twelve yojanas deep.”
Yojana
A unit of distance in Indian reckoning. There are three kinds, great, medium, and small: a great yojana is about eighty li; a medium yojana about sixty li; a small yojana about forty li.

[Mount Iron Enclosure] The iron mountain that encircles the salt sea and marks off a small world. [The seven treasures] The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:
“In that Buddha-land, the natural seven treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, tridacna, and carnelian — are combined to make its ground.”

[Tridacna (chē qú)] A rare organic gem, white as jade; it is the largest bivalve shellfish in the ocean, called the “king of shells,” and may reach 1.8 m in diameter. The Compendium of Materia Medica says:
“The chequ is a great shellfish of the sea; on its back are ridge-lines like the ruts of a cartwheel.”

[When Ānanda heard this, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: If that land has no Mount Sumeru, on what do the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three depend for their dwelling?]

When Ānanda heard this, he reverently asked the World-Honored One: If the Land of Utmost Bliss has no Mount Sumeru, then on what do the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three depend for their dwelling?

[On what do they depend for their dwelling] In ordinary Buddha-lands, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is on the flank of Mount Sumeru, and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is on its summit; both depend on the mountain for their dwelling. Ānanda, hearing the Buddha say that the Land of Utmost Bliss has no Mount Sumeru, therefore asked this question.
[The Buddha told Ānanda: On what do the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and even all the heavens of the realms of form and formlessness depend for their dwelling?]

The Buddha asked Ānanda in return: The Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and even all these heavens of the realm of form and the realm of formlessness — they are not on Mount Sumeru; on what, then, do they depend for their dwelling?

[All the heavens, on what do they depend for their dwelling] The Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three depend on Mount Sumeru for their dwelling and are called earth-dwelling heavens; all the heavens from the Yāma Heaven upward dwell in space and are called space-dwelling heavens.
[Ānanda said: It is brought about by the power of inconceivable karma.]
Ānanda reverently replied: They dwell in space; this is accomplished by reliance on the power of inconceivable karma.

[Inconceivable] Beyond the reach of the thought and speech of sentient beings. [Karma] What is done by body, speech, and mind. [The power of karma] The power of karma. Good karma has the power to produce the fruit of joy; evil karma has the power to produce the fruit of suffering.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: The inconceivable power of karma — can you know it? Your own karmic reward is inconceivable; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable; the roots of goodness of sentient beings are inconceivable; the sagely powers of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are likewise inconceivable. The beings of that land, by the power of their merit and goodness, dwell in the ground of the Buddha's practice, and by the Buddha's spiritual power, are able to be so.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda: The inconceivable power of karma — can you know it? Your own karmic reward is inconceivable; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable; the roots of goodness of sentient beings are inconceivable; the sagely powers of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are likewise inconceivable. Because the beings of the Land of Utmost Bliss dwell, by the power of their merit and goodness, in the ground of Amitābha Buddha's practice, and by the spiritual power of Amitābha Buddha, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three in the Land of Utmost Bliss are able to dwell in space.
[The ground of the practice] The ground accomplished by Amitābha Buddha's great vows, great practice, and great karma.

[Ānanda said: The karmic causes and fruits of retribution are inconceivable! Concerning this Dharma, I truly have no doubt. It is only to break the net of doubt for the sake of sentient beings in the future that I asked this question.]

Ānanda said to the Buddha: The karmic causes and fruits of retribution are inconceivable! Concerning the ability of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three in the Land of Utmost Bliss to dwell in space, I truly have no doubt at all. It is only to break the doubts of sentient beings in the future (since sentient beings in the future may raise this very question) that I asked this question.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: The awesome spiritual light of Amitābha Buddha is the most honored and foremost, and cannot be matched by the Buddhas of the ten directions. It universally illumines Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the east, and likewise in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below. The light of other Buddhas illumines one or two Buddha-lands, or a hundred or a thousand Buddha-lands. Only Amitābha Buddha's light universally illumines immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: The awesome spiritual light of Amitābha Buddha is the most honored and foremost, and cannot be matched by the Buddhas of the ten directions. The halo at his crown universally illumines Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the east, and Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the south, west, and north, and Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the four intermediate directions (southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast), above and below. The light of other Buddhas illumines one or two Buddha-lands, or a hundred or a thousand Buddha-lands. Only Amitābha Buddha's light universally illumines immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.

[The distance illumined by the light of the Buddhas accords with the greatness or smallness of the vows and merit they made when, as bodhisattvas, they sought the Way. When they become Buddhas, each obtains accordingly.]

The distance illumined by the light of the Buddhas accords with the greatness or smallness of the original vows and merit of each when, as bodhisattvas, they sought the Way; each differs. When they become Buddhas, each obtains accordingly.

[Amitābha Buddha's light is excellent and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a thousand koṭis of times; it is the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Amitābha Buddha is also named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, and also named the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Peerless Light; and also named the Light of Wisdom, Ever-Shining Light, Pure Light, Joyful Light, Light of Liberation, Light of Peace and Stability, Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and Inconceivable Light.]

Amitābha Buddha's light is exceedingly excellent, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a thousand koṭis of times; he is the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Amitābha Buddha is also named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, and also named the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Peerless Light; and also named the Light of Wisdom, Ever-Shining Light, Pure Light, Joyful Light, Light of Liberation, Light of Peace and Stability, Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and Inconceivable Light.

[The most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas] The Sutra of Amitābha Buddha, the Three Buddhas, the Sagely Tower, the Buddha's Altar, and the Crossing over of Human Beings, Spoken by the Buddha (the Wu translation) says:
“The light of Amitābha Buddha is lovely and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a hundred thousand koṭis of times.
He is the king among Buddhas, the most honored among lights.”

[Light such as this universally illumines all the worlds of the ten directions. If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, their defilements are extinguished and goodness is born, and body and mind become gentle. If they are in the three paths, in places of extreme suffering, and see this light, all their torment ceases, and at the end of life they all attain liberation. If there are sentient beings who hear of his light, his awesome spiritual merit, and day and night proclaim and praise it with a sincere heart without cease, then according to their wishes they will be born in that land.]
Light such as this

universally illumines all the worlds of the ten directions. If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, evil defilements are extinguished and roots of goodness are born, and body (conduct) and mind (intent) become gentle. If they are in the places of extreme suffering of the three evil paths and see this light, all their pain and torment cease, and at the end of life they all attain liberation. If there are sentient beings who hear of his light and awesome spiritual merit, and day and night proclaim and praise it with a sincere heart without cease, then according to their wishes they will be born in that land (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss).

[Lifespan and multitudes] Lifespan and the number of people. [Immeasurable lifespan and multitudes] Amitābha Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable, and the lifespan and the number of the people of that land (bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans) are likewise immeasurable.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: Amitābha Buddha's lifespan is long and cannot be reckoned or measured. The multitudes of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans — their lifespans and their numbers are likewise so, and cannot be known by reckoning or simile.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda: Amitābha Buddha's lifespan is long and cannot be reckoned or measured. The multitudes of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans — their lifespans and their numbers are likewise so, and cannot be known by reckoning or simile.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“The Buddha said to Ānanda: Moreover, the lifespan of the Buddha Immeasurable Life is long and cannot be reckoned or measured. Do you not know? Suppose that immeasurable sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions all obtained human bodies and were all made into śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; that they all gathered together in one place, concentrated their minds in meditative thought, exhausted their powers of intellect, and for a hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas together calculated and reckoned the length of that lifespan — they could not exhaust it or know its limit. The lifespans of the multitudes of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, gods, and humans are likewise so, and cannot be known by reckoning or simile. Moreover, the numbers of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are hard to measure and cannot be told; their spiritual wisdom is penetrating and their awesome power is sovereign, so that they can hold all worlds in the palm of the hand.”
